annotations.text:
The range slider is the one that earns its place: transcribing 2h17m is eight minutes, and most of a service is not worth analysing. Everything else here already exists as a setting — this just asks before the run instead of after.

No credits, no plan banner, no genre picker. Chop Shop has none of those.

The clips become the screen. Today they are a narrow column beside a big source player, which is backwards — the source is context, the clips are the work.

The grid is vertical because the output is vertical.

Opening one clip: player, Claude's reason, the transcript around it, and the four things you can actually do with it. Export to Premiere is real and already built.

No publish-to-social, no upscale — inventing those in a mockup only disappoints later.

Edit on a clip card lands here, not in the old studio view. The transcript is the edit surface: strike a word and it leaves the render.

Everything in the right rail already exists in the code (cuts, zooms, subject tracking, B-roll, music, looks) and has just never had anywhere to live. Four tracks, because this edits one clip.

Editing mode, built as a real NLE rather than a preview with tracks under it.

Project bin with columns, source and program monitors side by side, effect controls with keyframes on a timeline, Lumetri values, audio meters. Below: the eleven-tool palette on its real keys, track targeting, per-track mute/solo/lock, clip labels coloured by source, a transition sitting on a cut, and a zoom bar.

This is the larger of the two builds by a wide margin. Direct manipulation is the whole thing here: drag-to-trim, ripple, snapping and slip have to feel right, or it is worse than not having them.
